title: Linear recurrence from a rational power series
statement:
Let $K$ be a field [def-weil-field], $C(T)=\sum_{n\geq0}c_nT^n\in K[[T]]$ a formal power series [def-weil-formal-power-series], and $P,Q\in K[T]$ polynomials [def-weil-polynomial-ring] with $Q(0)=1$ and $QC=P$ in $K[[T]]$ [def-weil-polynomial-as-power-series]. Write $Q=\sum_{j\geq0}b_jT^j$ with $b_j=[T^j]Q$ [def-weil-polynomial-coefficient], so $b_0=1$; let $d=\max(\deg Q,1)$, and let $m\geq0$ be an integer with $[T^N]P=0$ for every $N\geq m+d$ (for instance $m=\deg P+1$, or $m=0$ when $P=0$). Put $a_i=b_{d-i}$ for $0\leq i\leq d-1$. Then $(c_n)$ satisfies the linear recurrence of order $d$ with coefficients $a_0,\ldots,a_{d-1}$ from the index $m$ on [def-weil-eventual-linear-recurrence]:
$$
c_{n+d}+a_{d-1}c_{n+d-1}+\cdots+a_0c_n=0\qquad(n\geq m).
$$
(If $Q=1$, then $d=1$, $a_0=0$, and the conclusion says $c_{n+1}=0$ for $n\geq m$.)

source.place: Ch. II, §27, proof of Lemma 27.9, p. 157 (quoting Bourbaki, Algèbre, IV.5, Exercise 3(a): f lies in k(t) iff its coefficients satisfy a linear relation λ_1a_n+…+λ_ra_{n+r-1}=0 for all n≥d; stated, not proved); the direction 'rational implies recurrence'

proof.text: Since $b_0=Q(0)=1$, the polynomial $Q$ is nonzero. By the definition of polynomial degree in [def-weil-polynomial-ring] and [def-weil-polynomial-coefficient], $d=\max(\deg Q,1)$ is an integer with $d\geq1$ and $b_j=0$ whenever $j>d$: otherwise $j$ would exceed the largest index with a nonzero coefficient.

source.place: Proof, final paragraph, direction (1) implies (3); elementary coefficient calculation supplied by the worker (Milne LEC, p. 157, quotes Bourbaki IV.5 Exercise 3(a) without proof)

proof.text: Fix an arbitrary integer $n\geq m$ and put $N=n+d$. Then $N\geq d$ and $N\geq m+d$, so $[T^N]P=0$ by the given hypothesis. The coefficient-preserving polynomial inclusion [def-weil-polynomial-as-power-series] and the Cauchy product formula in [def-weil-formal-power-series], applied to $QC=P$, give $0=[T^N]P=\sum_{j=0}^{N}b_jc_{N-j}$. The terms with $j>d$ vanish by Step 1. Since $b_0=1$, this is $c_{n+d}+\sum_{j=1}^{d}b_jc_{n+d-j}=0$.

source.place: Proof, final paragraph, direction (1) implies (3); elementary coefficient calculation supplied by the worker (Milne LEC, p. 157, quotes Bourbaki IV.5 Exercise 3(a) without proof)

proof.text: The substitution $i=d-j$ is a bijection from $1\leq j\leq d$ to $0\leq i\leq d-1$. Its summand is $b_jc_{n+d-j}=b_{d-i}c_{n+i}=a_ic_{n+i}$, by the given definition of $a_i$. Reordering the finite sum in Step 2 therefore gives $c_{n+d}+\sum_{i=0}^{d-1}a_ic_{n+i}=0$. As $n\geq m$ was arbitrary and $d\geq1$, this is precisely the recurrence of [def-weil-eventual-linear-recurrence].

source.place: Proof, final paragraph, direction (1) implies (3); elementary coefficient calculation supplied by the worker (Milne LEC, p. 157, quotes Bourbaki IV.5 Exercise 3(a) without proof)

proof.text: The suggested index choices and the constant-denominator case require no exclusions. If $P\ne0$, the definition of degree [def-weil-polynomial-coefficient] makes $[T^N]P=0$ for $N>\deg P$, so $m=\deg P+1$ has the required vanishing; if $P=0$, every coefficient is zero and $m=0$ works. If $Q=1$, its coefficients in [def-weil-polynomial-ring] are $b_0=1$ and $b_j=0$ for $j\geq1$; thus $d=1$, $a_0=b_1=0$, and Step 3 reads $c_{n+1}=0$ for every $n\geq m$, including $P=0,m=0$.
